title: Two threads, one cache line

prereqs.why: False sharing is a direct consequence of coherence being maintained per line rather than per variable.
The whole problem is that the unit of coherence is 64 bytes and not 8.
Every fix here is an alignment or layout change, so you need to be able to reason about where things land.

statement:
Two threads each count their own events. The counters live in one struct:

```cpp
struct Counters {
    std::atomic<long> a;   // thread 1 only ever touches this
    std::atomic<long> b;   // thread 2 only ever touches this
};
Counters shared;
```

Each thread runs a tight loop doing `shared.a++` or `shared.b++` ten million times. The threads are on different physical cores, and **neither ever reads or writes the other's counter**.

Measured on a machine with 64-byte cache lines:

```
one thread alone, incrementing a      0.09 s
both threads, as written above        2.80 s
```

Thirty times slower for running two independent counters in parallel. The cause is **false sharing**: `a` and `b` are 8 bytes apart, so they occupy the same cache line, and the line ping-pongs between the two cores' private caches on every increment.

**Which of the following would substantially fix it?** Select all that apply.
hints: The unit the hardware moves between cores is the line, not the variable. What has to be true of two addresses for them to be in different lines?
Ask of each option: does it change which cache line each counter lands in? Some options change the code a great deal and the layout not at all.
One option removes the sharing entirely rather than spacing it out. That is usually the right answer in real code.

options: Pad the struct so each counter sits in its own line: `struct Counters { alignas(64) std::atomic<long> a; alignas(64) std::atomic<long> b; };`
Give each thread a plain local `long`, increment that in the loop, and add it to the shared atomic once at the end.
Change both counters from `std::atomic<long>` to plain `long`.
Use `std::memory_order_relaxed` on the increments instead of the default `seq_cst`.
